problem: Robot control via joysticks is burdensome, and single-modality (verbal or gesture) interfaces are ambiguous ('go there' without pointing). Learning multimodal human-robot interaction from real demonstrations needs a lot of data and suffers from distributional shift under limited demonstrations.
motivation: Non-experts need intuitive ways to teach and command legged robots like dogs respond to cues. Physical demonstration is costly for users, so the system must learn from very little interaction data (under 1 hour) while remaining robust at deployment.
key_idea: Collect few luring-based (teaching rod) demonstrations with gestures and speech, reconstruct scenes in simulation for DAgger-style data aggregation with a local expert, and use progressive goal cueing to keep commands aligned with robot progress.
insight: Data aggregation with scene reconstruction and domain randomization fixes distribution shift (DAgger vs BC: +18.6% SR, -24.6% error), and progressive goal cueing adds a further +13.7% SR and -15.2% error by keeping command-state alignment. The modality ablation shows speech and gesture are complementary: gesture only yields 19.83% SR, and verbal only gives 1.68 m error, versus 0.43 m with both.
method: Locomotion controller: pretrained agile velocity tracker (50 Hz, Isaac Gym, RL, obstacle jumping) plus velocity planner converting a navigation goal g into heading and yaw commands; the System-1 module.

Luring data collection: one person gives speech and gestures while another guides the robot with a teaching rod; record robot state, rod goal g*, gesture keypoints, speech, obstacles at 10 Hz in a global frame.

Data aggregation: reconstruct scenes in sim, replay commands, train the high-level navigation policy pi_g (outputs goal in robot frame) with a local expert giving corrective goals toward g* under domain randomization (pushes, mass, terrain scaling, binary obstacle map, distractors).
Progressive goal cueing: hold each command until the robot reaches the current goal before advancing, applied with 50% probability per step and fading as the policy improves.
Interaction augmentation: Gaussian noise on gesture keypoints; GPT generates N_v=20 paraphrases of each verbal command.
Multimodal input: Silero VAD + Whisper + text encoder for speech; 6 upper-body mocap keypoints (OptiTrack) as unit direction vectors plus human yaw for gesture.
Fast user adaptation: fine-tune on ~4.5 min of data from a new user.

setting.backbone: Small navigation policy (trained from scratch with DAgger-style aggregation) + RL-trained velocity tracker; Whisper and a pretrained text encoder for speech; GPT for paraphrasing
setting.training_data: Under 1 hour of human-guided luring demonstrations across six scenarios (one user), plus LLM paraphrases and sim aggregation; 4.5 min per new user for adaptation
setting.observation: Mocap-based robot state, gesture keypoints, speech transcription, and heightmap/binary obstacle map from pre-measured obstacle poses
setting.action_space: High-level navigation goal in the robot frame, converted to velocity commands for a low-level joint-level locomotion policy
setting.privileged: Motion-capture for robot state, human pose and obstacle poses with pre-measured obstacle dimensions; controlled environment

results: LURE reaches 97.15% average success across six scenarios, beating DAgger (data aggregation without progressive cueing), BC and GAIL. Aggregation gives +18.6% SR over BC, cueing another +13.7%. Adaptation with 4.5 min raises novel-user SR from 74.00/80.83/64.33% to 95.33/91.50/98.67%. A real robot completed a multi-obstacle course five times in a row.
limitations: No zero-shot generalization across users; gesture augmentation is noise only, and adaptation is needed per user
Progressive cueing only retimes replayed human data instead of generating new human behavior for novel states
Requires mocap suits and pre-measured primitive obstacles, so it is restricted to controlled environments
